title: Mock Exam 9: Art, Archaeology & the Past

listeningParts.title: Enquiring about an archaeology dig
listeningParts.contextDescription: A student phones a heritage trust about volunteering on a summer archaeological excavation.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Northvale Heritage Trust, Gemma speaking.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Hi, I'm calling about the summer excavation at Castle Hill. I saw on your website that you're looking for volunteers, and I'm really interested.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Lovely. Yes, we're recruiting now. Can I ask a little about you first? Have you any experience of archaeology?

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Not on a real excavation, but I'm studying history at university, and I did a short course on archaeological methods last year, so I know the basics.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: That's fine. We take complete beginners as well. Everyone gets a full day's training at the start, covering how to use the tools, how to record what you find and, very importantly, health and safety.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Great. Could you tell me a bit about the site? The website said it was a Roman fort.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: That's what we thought originally, because Roman coins were found there in the nineteenth century. But last year's excavation found that the fort was actually built on top of a much older settlement, from the Iron Age, about two and a half thousand years ago. So this year, the main aim is to find out more about the people who lived there before the Romans arrived.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fascinating. When does the excavation take place?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: It runs for four weeks, from the seventh of July to the first of August. Volunteers can sign up for one week or more. Most people do two weeks, which gives you time to really learn the techniques.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I think two weeks would be good. Probably the first two, because I have a family holiday at the end of July.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Perfect. The first fortnight tends to be when we open the new trenches, so it's a good time to start. The working day runs from eight thirty until four thirty, Monday to Friday, with an hour for lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Is there a cost to volunteer?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: There's a contribution of sixty pounds per week, which covers training, insurance and the use of tools. For students, it's reduced to forty pounds a week, so you'd pay eighty in total.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That's fine. What about accommodation? I'll be coming from quite far away.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Some volunteers camp at a farm about a mile from the site, which is free, but very basic. There's also a youth hostel in the village, which offers a discounted rate of twenty-two pounds a night for our volunteers. You'd need to book that yourself, though, because it gets busy in the summer.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: I'll probably go for the hostel. What should I bring?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Strong boots are essential, preferably with steel toe caps. Also a sun hat, sun cream and plenty of water, because there's very little shade on the hill. We provide most of the tools, but many volunteers like to have their own trowel. If you want to buy one, make sure it's a proper archaeological trowel, not a garden one.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. And what happens to the things that are found?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Every find is cleaned, labelled and recorded on site. Then the important ones go to the county museum, where specialists study them. At the end of each week, the site director gives a talk about what's been discovered, and that's open to the public too.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: That sounds amazing. How do I apply?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: There's an application form on the website. You'll need to include the name of someone who can give you a reference; for a student, your tutor would be ideal. Applications close on the thirtieth of May.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I give you my name now, so you know to expect it?

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.text: It's Rebecca Lowenthal. L-O-W-E-N-T-H-A-L.

dialogue.speaker: Officer
dialogue.text: Thanks, Rebecca. I'll look out for your form. One last thing: if you have any allergies, particularly to insect stings, please mention them on the form, because the site is close to some beehives.

listeningParts.title: A tour of a restored historic house
listeningParts.contextDescription: A guide introduces visitors to a historic house that has recently been restored.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Welcome to Ashcombe Hall. My name's Simon, and I'll be your guide this morning. The house reopened to the public in March, after a restoration project that took six years and cost eleven million pounds. Before we go inside, I'll give you some background and explain what you'll see.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The house was built in the 1720s for a wealthy merchant, Sir Edward Ashcombe, who made his fortune in the textile trade. It remained in the Ashcombe family for nearly two hundred years. Then, after the First World War, the family could no longer afford to keep it. It was sold and used as a school for boys until the 1970s, and then it stood empty for almost twenty years. By the time the Trust bought it, the roof was leaking badly, and some of the ceilings had collapsed.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The aim of the restoration was not simply to make the house look as it did in the eighteenth century. The conservators decided that each room would show a different period in the house's history. So, as you go round, you'll see rooms as they were in the 1720s, the 1850s, and even one classroom from the school period, complete with old wooden desks.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: One of the biggest challenges was the Great Hall, which is where we'll start. Its painted ceiling had been covered with white paint when the house was a school, probably because the headmaster thought the images were unsuitable for boys. Conservators spent nearly two years removing the paint, layer by layer, using small scalpels and special solvents. The scenes underneath, showing figures from Greek mythology, were in remarkably good condition.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: From the Great Hall, we'll go up to the Long Gallery on the first floor, where you can see portraits of the Ashcombe family. Most of these were sold when the family left, and the Trust has managed to buy back about half of them, from collectors and auction houses around the world. The portrait of Lady Margaret Ashcombe was found in a private house in Canada, and it was returned only last year.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Many visitors say their favourite part of the house is the servants' quarters in the basement. In the eighteenth century, around thirty servants worked here, and the kitchens show you just how hard their lives were. We know a lot about them because the housekeeper's account books survived, recording everything from wages to the price of candles. There's an interactive display where you can find out about individual servants and what happened to them.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Outside, the gardens are still being restored, using a plan from 1760 that was discovered in the county archives. At the moment, only the walled kitchen garden is open, and it's growing the same varieties of fruit and vegetables that would have been grown at the time. The rest of the garden should open next spring.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A few practical points. Photography is allowed everywhere except in the Long Gallery, because flash can damage the paintings. Please don't touch the furniture or the walls, and stay behind the ropes. The tour takes about an hour and a quarter. Afterwards, the tearoom in the old stables serves lunch, and the shop sells books about the house and its restoration.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: On the second floor, you'll also find a small exhibition about the restoration itself, with photographs showing the state of the house when the Trust bought it, and some of the tools the conservators used. There's a short film too, which many visitors find surprisingly moving, because it shows how close the house came to being lost.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: And if you enjoy your visit, you might like to know that the Trust is always looking for volunteers to work as room guides. It's a great way to learn more about the house, and full training is provided. Right, let's go in.

listeningParts.title: Researching art forgery
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two art history students, Marta and Ollie, discuss their research project on art forgery with their supervisor.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: So, Marta and Ollie, you've chosen art forgery for your project. What drew you to that topic?

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: I watched a documentary about a forger who fooled experts for decades, and I wanted to understand how that was possible. It seems strange that people who've spent their whole lives studying art could be deceived.

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: And for me, it raises interesting questions about value. If a forgery is so good that nobody can tell the difference, why is it worth so much less than the original?

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: That's a philosophical question as well as a practical one. Let's start with the practical side. How do experts detect forgeries?

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: There are three main approaches. The first is connoisseurship, which means experts judging a work by its style, the way the artist painted, the brushwork and so on. The second is provenance research: tracing the history of who has owned the painting since it was made. And the third is scientific analysis of the materials.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Which do you think is the most reliable?

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: We disagree on that, actually. I think science is the most reliable, because you can't argue with chemistry. For example, if a painting supposedly from the seventeenth century contains a pigment that wasn't invented until the nineteenth century, it must be a fake.

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: But science can only prove that something is a fake. It can't prove that a painting is genuine. A clever forger can use old canvas and make their own paints from historical recipes. So I think provenance is more important. If there's a complete record of ownership going back to the artist, that's very strong evidence.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Though provenance documents can themselves be forged. One of the most famous forgers in Britain, John Myatt, worked with a man who created false records and even inserted fake documents into the archives of major museums.

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: Yes, we read about that. It's amazing how much effort went into it.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: What about connoisseurship? It's sometimes dismissed as too subjective.

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: It can be, but our reading suggested it's still essential, because it's often what raises suspicion in the first place. Experts look at a painting and feel that something isn't quite right, and that leads to further investigation.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, which case studies are you planning to use?

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: We're going to focus on Han van Meegeren, the Dutch forger who painted fake Vermeers in the 1930s and 1940s. What's interesting about him is that he was only caught because, after the Second World War, he was accused of selling a national treasure to the Nazi leader Hermann Göring. That was treason, so to save himself, he had to prove the painting was a fake he'd made himself.

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: And he actually painted another fake Vermeer in front of witnesses to prove he could do it.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: A wonderful story. Make sure you also discuss why the experts were fooled. Many critics have pointed out that his paintings don't look much like Vermeer to modern eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Ollie
dialogue.text: We think part of it was that experts wanted to believe. Van Meegeren painted religious scenes that filled a gap in Vermeer's known work, which experts had predicted might exist. So they were seeing what they hoped to see.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Excellent. That links to wider research on confirmation bias. For your second case study, I'd suggest something more recent, involving modern scientific methods.

dialogue.speaker: Marta
dialogue.text: We were thinking of the case where a painting was exposed because of radiocarbon dating of the canvas fibres, which showed they were too recent.

dialogue.speaker: Supervisor
dialogue.text: Good choice. And for the final section, return to Ollie's question about value. That would make a strong conclusion. Please send me an outline by the end of next week.

listeningParts.title: Cave art and the origins of creativity
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in an anthropology course on prehistoric cave art.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Today we're going to look at some of the oldest art in the world: the paintings and engravings made on cave walls during the Palaeolithic period, the Old Stone Age. These images raise fundamental questions about when and why humans began to create art, and what it tells us about the development of the human mind.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The modern study of cave art began in 1879, when a Spanish amateur archaeologist, Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola, was exploring the cave of Altamira in northern Spain. It was actually his eight-year-old daughter, Maria, who first noticed paintings of bison on the ceiling of a side chamber. When Sautuola published his findings, most experts refused to believe that prehistoric people could have produced such sophisticated work, and he was accused of having faked the paintings. It was only after similar paintings were found in France in the early 1900s that the experts accepted they were genuine, by which time Sautuola had died.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The most famous cave art site is probably Lascaux in south-western France, discovered in 1940 by four teenagers who were searching for their dog. Lascaux contains around six hundred paintings, mostly of animals such as horses, deer and cattle, many of them painted with great skill. The cave was opened to the public after the Second World War, but by the 1960s, the breath and body heat of more than a thousand visitors a day had caused algae and crystals to grow on the walls, and it was closed. Today, visitors see an exact replica built nearby.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: How do we know how old these paintings are? For paintings made with charcoal, researchers can use radiocarbon dating, which measures the decay of carbon in organic material. Using this method, the paintings at Chauvet Cave in France, discovered in 1994, were found to be around thirty-six thousand years old, far older than anyone had expected for such sophisticated work. They include images of lions, rhinoceroses and mammoths, animals that are rarely shown in later cave art.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: For a long time, it was assumed that cave art began in Europe. That assumption has now been overturned. In 2014, researchers used a technique called uranium-series dating, which measures the thin layers of mineral that form over paintings, to date hand stencils in caves on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. A hand stencil is made by placing a hand against the rock and blowing pigment around it. The Sulawesi stencils turned out to be at least forty thousand years old, and a painting of a wild pig found there has since been dated to over forty-five thousand years. This suggests that art may have developed in many places, or that the ability to make it was already present in the early humans who left Africa.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Even more controversially, some researchers have claimed that certain markings in Spanish caves are more than sixty-four thousand years old, which would mean they were made by Neanderthals rather than modern humans, since modern humans had not yet arrived in Europe. If confirmed, this would challenge the long-held view that symbolic thinking was unique to our species. However, other scientists have questioned the dating, and the debate continues.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Why did people make cave art? There are many theories. An early idea was 'art for art's sake', simply the pleasure of decoration. Another popular theory was hunting magic: by painting animals, people hoped to ensure success in the hunt. But studies of the bones found in caves show that the animals people actually ate were often different from those they painted. At Lascaux, for example, reindeer were the main food, yet they appear in only one painting.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: More recent theories focus on sound and ritual. Some researchers have found that paintings are often located in parts of caves with unusual acoustics, where echoes are particularly strong, suggesting that the spaces may have been used for ceremonies involving music or chanting. Others note that many of the images are in deep, dark and hard-to-reach parts of the caves, which would have been experienced by flickering lamplight, making the animals appear to move.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Whatever its purpose, cave art shows that, tens of thousands of years ago, humans were capable of abstract thought, planning and communicating through symbols, abilities that underlie language, religion and science. Next week, we'll look at the earliest musical instruments.

readingPassages.title: The terracotta army
paragraphs: In March 1974, a group of farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an in central China struck pieces of fired clay. At first they thought they had found fragments of an old water pot, but when archaeologists arrived to investigate, they realised that the farmers had uncovered something far more significant: part of a life-sized clay figure of a soldier. Over the following years, excavations revealed one of the most remarkable archaeological discoveries of the twentieth century, an army of thousands of terracotta warriors, buried for more than two thousand years to guard the tomb of China's first emperor.

The emperor, Qin Shi Huang, came to power as king of the state of Qin at the age of thirteen in 246 BC. Over the following twenty-five years, he conquered the other warring states that made up China at the time, and in 221 BC he declared himself the first emperor of a unified country. His achievements were enormous. He standardised writing, weights and measures and the width of cart axles, built thousands of kilometres of roads and began linking existing defensive walls into an early version of the Great Wall. But he was also a ruthless ruler, who is said to have ordered the burning of books that challenged his authority.

Work on the emperor's tomb began soon after he came to the throne and continued for decades. According to the historian Sima Qian, writing about a century later, around seven hundred thousand workers were involved. Sima Qian described an underground palace containing a model of the empire, with rivers of mercury that flowed mechanically, and crossbows set to fire automatically at anyone who broke in. For centuries, historians assumed these descriptions were exaggerated. However, modern scientific surveys have detected unusually high levels of mercury in the soil above the tomb, suggesting that at least part of the account may be accurate.

The terracotta army itself was found in pits about one and a half kilometres east of the burial mound. Archaeologists estimate that the three main pits contain around eight thousand soldiers, together with horses and wooden chariots. The figures were arranged in military formation, with archers at the front, infantry behind and chariots among them, apparently ready for battle. Most remarkably, no two faces appear to be exactly alike. The figures were made in sections using moulds, but the heads were finished individually by hand, giving each soldier a distinct appearance, and some researchers believe they may have been modelled on real people.

When they were made, the figures were brightly painted in red, green, blue, purple and other colours. Unfortunately, almost all of this paint has disappeared. When the figures are exposed to the dry air after centuries underground, the layer beneath the paint dries out and curls within minutes, and the colours flake off. This is one reason why excavation has proceeded slowly. Chinese archaeologists have worked with conservation experts from other countries to develop methods of preserving the paint, and some figures with their original colours have now been successfully preserved.

Excavating the soldiers has also revealed much about how the army was produced. Many figures carry the names of the workshop foremen who supervised their production, which allowed officials to trace and punish anyone responsible for poor workmanship. The real bronze weapons held by the soldiers, including swords, spearheads and crossbow triggers, were also inscribed with marks indicating where and when they were made. Some of the weapons were coated with a layer of chromium and remained remarkably sharp, although researchers now think the coating may have come from the lacquer of the wooden handles rather than from a deliberate treatment.

Perhaps the most intriguing question concerns the emperor's tomb itself, which has never been opened. The Chinese government has so far decided not to excavate it, partly out of respect, but mainly because archaeologists are concerned that they do not yet have the technology to protect what might be found inside, particularly any painted or organic materials. They point to the loss of the soldiers' colours as a warning. For now, the tomb remains sealed, and the secrets of the first emperor's underground palace continue to wait for a future generation.

readingPassages.title: Why do we value original art?
paragraphs: In 2017, a painting attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, known as Salvator Mundi, was sold at auction for four hundred and fifty million dollars, the highest price ever paid for a work of art. Only a few years earlier, however, the same painting had been sold for less than ten thousand dollars, when it was believed to be the work of one of Leonardo's followers. Nothing about the physical object had changed between the two sales, apart from careful restoration. What had changed was a belief about who had painted it. The case illustrates a question that has puzzled philosophers and psychologists alike: why do we place so much value on originality?

One obvious answer is rarity. There are fewer than twenty paintings generally accepted as Leonardo's, and any object that is unique and cannot be replaced will command a high price. But rarity alone cannot explain the dramatic fall in value that follows when a painting is shown to be a forgery. A convincing forgery may be just as rare as an original, since there may be only one copy, yet once its true origins are revealed, its value collapses, even though people may have admired it for years.

Psychologists have suggested that part of the answer lies in what is called essentialism: the tendency to believe that objects possess an invisible essence connected to their history. In a series of experiments, the psychologist Paul Bloom and his colleagues found that people place great value on objects that have been touched or owned by famous individuals, such as a sweater worn by a celebrity, and that this value falls sharply if the object has been washed. It is as if the person's essence has been transferred into the object through physical contact. An original painting, on this view, is valued partly because it was physically touched by the hand of the artist.

Another explanation emphasises performance. The philosopher Denis Dutton argued that we see works of art not simply as objects but as the outcome of human achievement, in the same way that we admire an athlete's record-breaking run. A forgery may look identical to an original, but it represents a different, and lesser, achievement: copying is not the same as creating. Just as we would feel cheated to discover that a marathon winner had taken a shortcut, we feel deceived when we learn that a painting is not what it claims to be.

A third factor concerns the role of expertise and social status. The art market depends on the judgements of experts, dealers and museums, and the label of a famous name acts as a guarantee of quality and an investment. Some critics argue that this system encourages people to respond to the label rather than to the work itself. In one experiment, participants were shown the same abstract paintings, but some were told the works were in a major museum while others were told they had been generated by a computer. The paintings labelled as museum works were rated as more beautiful, and brain scans showed greater activity in areas associated with pleasure.

Not all cultures, or all periods, have valued originality in the same way. In traditional Chinese painting, copying the works of earlier masters was regarded as an essential part of an artist's training and a way of showing respect, and skilled copies could be highly prized. In medieval Europe, many artists worked in teams within workshops, and the idea of the individual creative genius was much less important than it later became. Some historians argue that the modern obsession with originality emerged largely in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, along with the development of copyright law and the art market.

Digital technology is now challenging traditional ideas once again. High-resolution scanning and three-dimensional printing can produce copies of paintings that reproduce even the texture of the brushstrokes, so accurately that experts find them difficult to distinguish from the original without close examination. Some museums have begun displaying such copies, particularly when the originals are too fragile to travel. Whether audiences will come to accept these reproductions, or will continue to insist on the authentic object, may tell us a great deal about what we really value when we look at art.

readingPassages.title: Lost cities of the rainforest
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, many archaeologists believed that tropical rainforests were unable to support large, complex societies. The soils of the Amazon, for instance, are generally poor in nutrients, because heavy rainfall washes them away and most of the nutrients in the ecosystem are stored in the vegetation rather than the ground. On this view, the rainforest was a hostile environment in which people could survive only in small, mobile groups, and reports by early European explorers of large settlements along the Amazon were dismissed as exaggerations. The dense forest also made it extremely difficult to test these assumptions, since ruins could be hidden beneath the canopy only a few metres from a researcher without being seen.

This picture has been transformed by a technology called LiDAR, which stands for light detection and ranging. A LiDAR instrument, usually mounted on an aircraft or drone, fires hundreds of thousands of laser pulses per second towards the ground and measures how long each one takes to return. Although most pulses are reflected by leaves and branches, a small proportion pass through gaps in the canopy and reach the forest floor. By filtering out the vegetation using computer software, researchers can produce a detailed three-dimensional map of the ground surface, revealing features such as walls, roads and terraces that would be almost impossible to detect on foot.

Some of the most dramatic results have come from Central America. In 2018, a survey of more than two thousand square kilometres of forest in northern Guatemala revealed over sixty thousand previously unknown structures associated with the ancient Maya, including houses, palaces, defensive walls and raised roads connecting cities. On the basis of these results, researchers suggested that the population of the Maya lowlands at its height, around the eighth century, may have been between seven and eleven million people, several times higher than many earlier estimates. The surveys also revealed extensive systems of canals and terraced fields, showing that the Maya had transformed large areas of the landscape to produce food.

Similar discoveries have been made in the Amazon. In Bolivia, a LiDAR survey published in 2022 revealed settlements of the Casarabe culture, which flourished between around 500 and 1400 AD. The surveys showed large platforms and pyramid-like mounds, connected by raised roads running for several kilometres, together with reservoirs and canals for managing water. In the upper Amazon of Ecuador, researchers have mapped a network of settlements more than two thousand years old, linked by long, straight roads. These findings suggest that, contrary to earlier assumptions, some parts of the Amazon supported dense, organised populations long before the arrival of Europeans.

How did such societies manage to farm the poor soils of the rainforest? Part of the answer lies in a remarkable dark, fertile soil known as terra preta, Portuguese for 'black earth', found at many ancient sites in the Amazon. Unlike the surrounding soils, terra preta is rich in nutrients and organic matter, including charcoal, pottery fragments and food waste, and it remains fertile today, centuries after the settlements were abandoned. Researchers believe it was created, at least in part deliberately, by ancient communities who added charcoal and waste to the soil. Some scientists are now studying terra preta in the hope of developing methods for improving soils in tropical regions today.

The discoveries also raise questions about the history of the rainforest itself. If large areas were once cleared, farmed and managed, then parts of what appears to be untouched wilderness may in fact have been shaped by human activity. Many of the tree species most common in the Amazon today are ones that were useful to people, such as Brazil nut and cacao, which some researchers interpret as evidence of ancient forest management. When European diseases devastated indigenous populations after 1492, the forest may have grown back over abandoned fields and settlements, creating the impression of a pristine landscape.

Not all researchers accept the most dramatic interpretations. Some argue that population estimates based on counting structures are uncertain, since it is often impossible to know how many buildings were occupied at the same time. Others warn that the idea of a heavily populated ancient Amazon could be misused to justify modern deforestation, by suggesting that the forest has recovered before and will do so again. In my view, the evidence does not support such a conclusion: ancient societies managed the forest over centuries in ways that maintained its diversity, which is very different from the large-scale clearing for cattle ranching and agriculture that threatens the Amazon today.
